p: Darius I, the Persian king under whom Haggai and Zechariah preached. In this book Zerubbabel goes home in his reign.
b: The Darius of this story is Darius I, the king under whom Haggai and Zechariah preached and the temple was finished (Haggai 1:1; Ezra 6:15). Josephus, who retells this chapter, calls him Darius son of Hystaspes, made king after the Magi were killed (Antiquities 11.31). The order matters. Ezra 1-3 has Zerubbabel and Jeshua lead the return under Cyrus. 1 Esdras has already told Cyrus's decree (2:1-14) and the halt under Artaxerxes (2:15-25), and now places Zerubbabel's own journey under Darius (5:1-6). See the note on 5:70 for the knot this makes. Torrey (1910) argued that the tale itself was first told of the last Darius, shortly before Alexander, and only later joined to Zerubbabel.

a: from India to Ethiopia, in the 127 satrapies
p: The same span and the same number as the opening of Esther. Daniel counts 120 satraps.
b: Esther opens with a king "from India all the way to Cush, over 127 provinces" (Esther 1:1); Ethiopia is the Greek name for Cush, the land south of Egypt. Daniel has "one hundred twenty satraps" under a Darius (Daniel 6:1). A satrap was the governor of a great province of the Persian Empire. Darius I's own inscription at Behistun lists "twenty-three lands in all" (Behistun, section 6), so 127 is not the count of his own records; this book shares the number with Esther. The feast that opens a court tale is also how Esther begins (Esther 1:3-9).

p: Three young guards, a sleeping king, a contest of wisdom: a story of the same kind as Daniel and Esther.
b: The story is a court tale, like Joseph before Pharaoh, Daniel in Babylon and Esther in Susa: a Jew at a foreign court wins by wisdom and uses the king's favor for his people. Torrey (1910) argued that the contest was first a separate wisdom tale, written in Aramaic, that says nothing of the Jews before 4:42, and that a later hand set it into the history. Böhler (2014) reads the speeches on women and truth as one argument by a Jewish author. Josephus makes the third guard an old friend of the king who was "thought worthy to be guard of the king's body" (Antiquities 11.32).

p: One Greek verb runs through the whole contest, and the Plain gives it one English word.
b: The verb hyperischyō means "to be stronger than, to win out, to prevail." It is the word of each written answer (3:10-12), of each speech's close (3:23; 4:12) and of the crowd's final cry (4:41), so the Plain renders it "is strongest" every time, and the simple adjective ischyros "strong" (4:32, 34). The KJV varies it ("strongest," "excel," "mighty above all things"), which hides how the crowd's shout answers the question the guards first asked.

p: Purple clothes, gold cups, a gold chain: the honors Persian and later Greek kings gave favorites.
b: Purple dye was costly and was the color of royalty. Belshazzar promises purple and a gold chain to whoever reads the writing on the wall, and Daniel receives them (Daniel 5:7, 29); Mordecai leaves the king's presence in royal clothing (Esther 8:15); Pharaoh puts a gold chain on Joseph (Genesis 41:42). In 1 Maccabees the Seleucid king sends Jonathan purple and a gold brooch "such as is given to the Kinsmen of kings" (1 Maccabees 10:89). The Greek maniakēs, the "chain around his neck" here, is the word the Old Greek of Daniel 5:7 uses for the gold chain Belshazzar promises.

p: Not a blood relative: "Kinsman" was a court rank, as in 1 Maccabees.
b: Syngenēs, "relative," here names a court rank, not a family tie. 1 Maccabees uses it the same way of a Seleucid king's high officials ("Lasthenes our Kinsman," 1 Maccabees 11:31; compare 1 Maccabees 10:89). Josephus has Darius promise that the winner "shall be called my cousin" (Antiquities 11.35). The KJV's "Darius his cousin" is the older English for the same word.

a: but truth wins over all things
p: The third guard gives two answers. Was "truth" added later, or was it the point all along?
b: Three guards should give three answers, but the third writes two: women, and truth over all. His speech also has two parts, a long one on women (4:13-32) and a shorter one on truth (4:33-41). Dieter Böhler notes that the truth speech is widely seen as a later addition, sometimes even suspected of not being Jewish, and argues instead that only the two speeches together make one philosophical argument against the earlier speakers, with an idea of truth close to the Qumran texts. Torrey (1910), who thought the whole tale was not Jewish at first, counted the truth speech part of the original. On either view the story's teller makes truth the winner, and truth here is tied to God (4:40).

p: The Greek word here was later the title of Rome's consuls.
b: The list repeats 3:1-2 and adds hypatoi, "the highest ones." In Greek of the 100s BC and after, hypatos was the regular word for a Roman consul (1 Maccabees 15:16 uses it for the Roman consul Lucius). Here it means only the top officials. The word is the Greek writer's, not a Persian title.

a: It makes the mind of the king and the mind of the orphan one and the same
p: The guard's praise of wine is really a list of its dangers, as in Proverbs.
b: The first speech praises wine's strength by listing what it does: it leads the mind astray, makes king and orphan alike, wipes out memory of debt and duty, and ends in drawn swords. Proverbs says the same thing as a warning: "Wine is a mocker, and beer is a rowdy" (Proverbs 20:1); compare the drunk who wakes and goes looking for more (Proverbs 23:29-35) and Noah's drunkenness (Genesis 9:21). The Bible also praises wine as God's gift that makes the heart glad (Psalm 104:15). The speech sits between: wine is strong, but its strength is a kind of forgetting.

p: Ancient readers knew the drinking party that ends in a killing.
b: The setting is a royal drinking feast (3:1-3), so the guard's picture was close to home. The Bible tells of killings at feasts: Absalom has Amnon killed "when Amnon's heart is feeling good with the wine" (2 Samuel 13:28), and Holofernes is killed after his drinking (Judith 13:2, 15). The first speech never says wine is good; it says wine overpowers, and that is the point the third speaker will turn around.

a: They hold power over the earth and the sea and everything in them
p: Humans rule creation, as Genesis and Psalm 8 say; the king rules the humans.
b: The second guard starts from the place of human beings in creation, given rule over the fish of the sea, the birds and every living thing (Genesis 1:28; Psalm 8:6-8). Then he climbs one step: the king rules those rulers. His speech is an argument from command and obedience, and its key verbs (kill, let go, strike, build, plant, 4:7-9) recall the list of times in Ecclesiastes 3:2-3, here put into one man's mouth.

a: he lies back at the table, eats and drinks, and sleeps
p: The speech's best line is a joke: the strongest man does the least.
b: After the long list of what others do for the king, the guard notes that the king himself only reclines, eats, drinks and sleeps, guarded on every side. Readers have heard both praise and satire in this. The speaker means it as proof of power, but the story has just shown the king asleep while his guards plan a contest (3:3-9), and the third speaker will show him slapped by his concubine (4:30). A wise ruler in the Bible is the opposite of this picture (Deuteronomy 17:18-20; Ecclesiastes 10:16-17).

p: The guard's name comes in an aside, halfway through. Some think the story was first about an unnamed Jew.
b: The three guards are nameless in chapter 3. Only here, in a side remark, is the third called Zerubbabel, the grandson of King Jehoiachin who led the return in Ezra 2:2 and Haggai 1:1. Because the name appears so late, and because 5:5-6 ties the "wise words" to a confusing list of names, Torrey (1910) judged "this was Zerubbabel" a later addition, and the words "who spoke wise words" in 5:6 a gloss joining the tale to the list: in his view the contest was first told of a nameless young man. Read as the book stands, the aside is a storyteller's reveal. Josephus removes the problem by naming Zerubbabel before the contest begins (Antiquities 11.32).

a: Next the third began to speak
t: Compared with the Bible: how Zerubbabel got his mission
p: Ezra and Haggai never say how Zerubbabel came to lead. 1 Esdras supplies a story they do not have.
b: This goes beyond the 66 books. Ezra lists Zerubbabel first among those who came back (Ezra 2:2) and Haggai calls him governor of Judah (Haggai 1:1), but neither tells how he gained the post. The contest gives him a place at Darius's court and a personal commission from Darius, not from Cyrus (4:42-57). Orthodox Bibles print 1 Esdras (the Russian Synodal Bible as the second book of Ezra), and Mihăilă counts it among the books beyond the Hebrew canon that the Orthodox reckon, so there the episode stands in the Old Testament beside Ezra. Catholic and Protestant churches do not count the book as Scripture. In Ezra, which every Bible has, the return comes under Cyrus (Ezra 1:1-2:2); Swete for that reason called the story, in its present form, "certainly unhistorical."

t: Praise of women, or a joke?
p: Readers hear the women speech as praise, as satire on men, or as a warning. It is likely all three.
b: The speech says women give birth to kings, raise the vine growers, clothe men and give them glory (4:15-17); that men drop gold to gape at a beautiful woman, leave father and country for a wife, and rob and sail and face lions to bring home loot (4:18-25); and that many have lost their minds, become slaves and sinned because of women (4:26-27). Some readers take it as an honest tribute to women's power, others as court humor at men's expense, others as a warning like Ecclesiastes 7:26 and Solomon's wives who "bent his heart" (1 Kings 11:3-4). Proverbs 31:10-31 is the Bible's fullest praise of a woman. The speech does not claim women are good, only strong; it ends by calling them, with the rest, "unjust" beside truth (4:37).

a: he sticks close to his own wife
p: Genesis 2:24 in a court speech, with the same Greek verb root.
b: Genesis says "a man leaves his father and his mother and sticks close to his wife" (Genesis 2:24). The Greek of Genesis has proskollaō, and Jesus' quotation in Matthew 19:5 has kollaō, the verb used here. The guard adds "who raised him" and "his own country," and turns the creation line into proof that women rule men. Readers of Genesis and Matthew hear in it a calling; here it is a loss of power.

a: he lets go of his life
p: The Greek idiom is used of dying; here it may mean giving up his life for her or spending it on her.
b: Aphiēsi tēn psychēn is literally "lets go the soul." The Greek Bible uses the same words for dying: Rachel dies "in letting go her soul" (Genesis 35:18 in the Greek). Here it may mean he gives up his life for his wife, or spends his life on her. The KJV takes it as "to spend his life with his wife." The Plain keeps the plain words, which allow each sense.

p: The king's concubine, named by this book and by Josephus, who gives her father another name.
b: This book calls Apame the king's concubine and "daughter of the admired Bartacus." Josephus calls her "Apame, the daughter of Rabsases Themasius, his concubine" (Antiquities 11.54). The Greek verb etheōroun can be "I used to watch" or "they used to see"; the KJV ("did I see"), like the Plain, takes it as the speaker's own memory. The scene of a woman taking a crown and slapping the king is the speech's comic peak: the strongest man on earth sweet-talks her to make up (4:31).

a: It wheels around the ring of the sky and hurries back to its own place in one day
p: As in Ecclesiastes and Psalm 19, the sun's daily run shows the power of the one who made it.
b: The truth speech begins with creation: the great earth, the high sky, the fast sun. Ecclesiastes says the sun "pants its way back to its place" (Ecclesiastes 1:5), and Psalm 19 has it run its loop from one edge of the sky to the other (Psalm 19:5-6). The point comes in 4:35: the maker of these is great, and truth is greater still. This is the Bible's ancient picture of the sky, which turns around the earth; the speaker's argument does not depend on it.

p: Greek alētheia: what is real, true and reliable. Hebrew emet adds "faithfulness."
b: The Greek alētheia means what is true and real, the opposite of a lie or an illusion. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Hebrew emet, which leans toward reliability and faithfulness ("the LORD's faithfulness is forever," Psalm 117:2, where the Greek has alētheia). The Plain gives the word one English rendering, "truth," in every verse of the speech, and also at 5:40, where the same word names the Thummim. In this speech truth is almost a person: it lives, rules, judges and has no favorites (4:38-40). See the topic.

p: The Greek "him" is masculine, so it points to God, not to truth, which is feminine.
b: Truth (alētheia) is a feminine noun, and the speech calls it "her" in 4:39-40. Here the pronoun is masculine (met' autou), so it most likely means the one "who does these things" (4:35): God. The KJV has "with it," making it truth. Either way, the line echoes the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:4, "a faithful God, and there is no injustice." (English has no grammatical gender, so the Plain says "truth" or "it" for the feminine pronouns.)

p: Greek adikos, "not right, not just": the three earlier answers are all judged by truth.
b: Adikos is the opposite of dikaios, "right, just." The speaker turns on everything praised so far: wine, the king, women and all humankind are unjust, and there is no truth in them. The KJV says "wicked"; the Plain uses "unjust" every time (4:36, 37, 39, 40) to keep one English word for the Greek one. The thought is close to Paul's "Let God be true, and every human being a liar" (Romans 3:4), which echoes Psalm 116:11.

p: "The truth of the Lord remains forever" is the Greek of Psalm 117:2.
b: The verb menei, "stays, remains," is the one the Greek Psalter uses: "and the truth of the Lord remains forever" (Greek Psalm 116:2, which is Psalm 117:2 in the Hebrew and English count; the site's Plain from the Hebrew reads "the LORD's faithfulness is forever"). Isaiah 40:8 says the same of God's word. The speech gives truth what the Bible gives God himself: endurance, life and rule forever.

a: no playing favorites and no bribe
p: What Deuteronomy says of God, the speech says of truth.
b: Moses says of the LORD, "He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17). The Greek here has lambanein prosōpa, "to receive faces," the Greek Bible's idiom for favoritism (Leviticus 19:15; Galatians 2:6), and diaphora, which can mean "distinctions" or "bribes" (KJV "rewards"). The judge who looks at faces or takes gifts is the Bible's picture of injustice; truth does neither.

a: keeps away from everything unjust and evil
p: The Greek can mean truth avoids evil, or that it does justice on the wicked.
b: The words ta dikaia poiei apo pantōn tōn adikōn are compressed. The KJV and the Plain read "does what is just (and keeps away) from all the unjust," with a verb of separating understood. Others read "does justice from (upon) all the unjust," that is, truth carries out judgment on them, which fits 4:40, "In its judging."
orig: τὰ δίκαια ποιεῖ ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἀδίκων

a: It has the strength, the royal power, the authority and the majesty of all the ages
p: The words David's prayer gives to God, the speech gives to truth, and then it blesses "the God of truth."
b: David prays, "To you, LORD, belong the greatness and the might, the beauty, the victory and the majesty... Yours, LORD, is the kingdom" (1 Chronicles 29:11). The truth speech gives truth strength, royal power, authority and majesty, then ends by blessing "the God of truth," as the Greek of Psalm 31:5 (Psalm 30:6 in the Greek count) calls the LORD ho theos tēs alētheias, where the site's Plain from the Hebrew El emet has "faithful God." The ending keeps truth under God: it is his. The ending that later copies added to the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:13 in the KJV) has the same shape of praise.

a: Blessed be the God of truth!
t: Claude's theory: truth as a figure like Wisdom
p: A suggestion, labeled as mine: the speech treats truth the way Proverbs treats Wisdom.
b: This is Claude's reading, not a church's teaching. Proverbs 8 and the Wisdom of Solomon 7 make Wisdom almost a person beside God, older than creation, ruling kings, and loved more than gold (Proverbs 8:10-31; Wisdom of Solomon 7:7-14, 25-26). The truth speech follows the same pattern: truth is praised above the things kings and lovers prize (compare 4:18-19 with Proverbs 8:11), and it lives and reigns. Christian readers will think of John, where the Word is "full of grace and truth" and Jesus says "I am the way, the truth and the life" (John 14:6). Böhler's reading of truth as a Jewish theme close to Qumran overlaps with this. Torrey (1910) also counted the tale with the wisdom writing of its time, though he thought it was not Jewish at first.
r: Proverbs 8:10-31; Wisdom of Solomon 7:7-14; John 1:14; John 14:6

a: Great is truth, and it is strongest!
p: The Latin of this cry became a proverb: "Great is truth, and it prevails."
b: The Latin Vulgate, where this book is 3 Esdras, reads magna veritas et praevalet, "great is truth, and it prevails." With est added, magna est veritas et praevalet is what Swete called "the immortal proverb" that this story gave the world. He notes that the future form, praevalebit, "it will prevail," has no support in the texts: the Latin has the present. Josephus has the people say that "it was truth alone that had immutable strength" (Antiquities 11.57).

a: Remember the vow you made to build Jerusalem
p: No other source says Darius vowed to rebuild Jerusalem. In Ezra, he finds Cyrus's decree instead.
b: Zerubbabel's request rests on a vow Darius made when he became king. Ezra knows nothing of it; there Darius searches the archives, finds Cyrus's decree and orders the work done (Ezra 6:1-12; in this book, 1 Esdras 6:22-33). Josephus also has Darius vow, before he was king, to send the vessels back if he gained the throne (Antiquities 11.31). In the story, the vow lets the young man ask for nothing for himself: he holds the king to his own word, as truth would.

p: This book has already sent the vessels home with Samanassar (2:10-14). Here they are still in Babylon.
b: In 2:10-14 Cyrus hands the temple vessels to his treasurer, and "Samanassar brought them up" to Jerusalem (as Ezra 1:7-11). Here Cyrus only "set aside" the vessels and vowed to send them, and Darius sends them (4:57). The book sets the two accounts side by side without comment. Torrey (1910) took clashes like this as signs that the contest story was set into the history by a later hand. Josephus has Darius vow to send the vessels to Jerusalem (Antiquities 11.31) and Zerubbabel ask him to restore them (11.58).

a: The Edomites set it on fire
t: Compared with the Bible: who burned the temple?
p: 2 Kings and Jeremiah say Nebuchadnezzar's officer burned it. The Edomites are blamed only here.
b: This conflicts with the 66 books in detail. 2 Kings 25:9 and Jeremiah 52:13 say Nebuzaradan, Nebuchadnezzar's commander, "set the LORD's house on fire." The Bible does remember Edom's part in Jerusalem's fall: Obadiah 11-14 accuses Edom of standing by and looting, and Psalm 137:7 asks the LORD to remember "against the people of Edom / the day of Jerusalem." 1 Esdras (in Codex Alexandrinus; Vaticanus reads "the Jews," see the variant) turns that memory into the burning itself. Readers who hold the book as Scripture can take "burned" loosely, of those who joined in the destruction; others read it as a later Jewish grievance against the Edomites (Idumeans) of the 100s BC.

p: A title for God used when Jews spoke to or about foreign kings.
b: The young man calls God "the King of heaven" before Darius, and blesses "the King of heaven" again in 4:58. Nebuchadnezzar uses the same title at the end of his madness (Daniel 4:37), and Tobit uses it (Tobit 13:7). It sets God above every king of earth, which is exactly the answer to the second guard's speech.

p: Ezra calls the region "Beyond the River." "Coele-Syria and Phoenicia" is the name it bore in the Greek period.
b: The Persian name for the province west of the Euphrates was "Beyond the River" (Ezra 4:10-11; 8:36). "Coele-Syria and Phoenicia," literally "Hollow Syria," is the name of the region under the Ptolemies and Seleucids, as in 2 Maccabees: "governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia" (2 Maccabees 3:5). 1 Esdras uses it in 2:20-23 too. So the book uses the name of its own Greek age, not of the Persian period it describes.

a: as they are commanded to offer seventeen
p: No law of Moses asks for seventeen offerings a day. The meaning of the number is unknown.
b: The Greek says only "as they have a command to offer seventeen." The law of the daily offering asks for two lambs a day, one in the morning and one at evening (Numbers 28:3-8; Exodus 29:38-42), and the festival offerings vary by day (Numbers 28-29). Seventeen fits none of these, and no other source explains it. The KJV keeps "seventeen"; a word may have dropped out. Josephus does not give the number.

a: Victory is from you, wisdom is from you
p: Zerubbabel thanks God for wisdom just as Daniel did after he read the king's dream.
b: Daniel blesses the God of his fathers "because you have given me wisdom and power" (Daniel 2:23). Zerubbabel's prayer has the same parts: wisdom comes from God, the glory is God's, and the winner is only a servant (Greek oiketēs, a household servant). The court contest has been won, but the prayer gives the victory back to God.

p: Greek despota, the word for a master of slaves, here God as Lord of Israel's ancestors.
b: Despotēs is the master of a household and its slaves. It answers "your household servant" in 4:59. The same address is used to God in Simeon's song (Luke 2:29) and in the church's prayer (Acts 4:24). The Greek says "of the fathers," not "of our fathers."

p: Aphesis is the Greek Bible's word for the Jubilee "release."
b: The pair anesis and aphesis mean "relief" and "release." In the Greek of Leviticus 25:10, aphesis is the release of the Jubilee year, when people return to their land ("proclaim release in the land," Leviticus 25:10). In the New Testament the same word is "forgiveness" and "release to the captives" (Luke 4:18). For exiles allowed to go home, the Jubilee word is fitting.

p: The verb means to drink deep. The tale that began by putting wine in its place ends with a week of it.
b: Kōthōnizomai comes from kōthōn, a drinking cup, and means to drink freely at a party. The KJV softens it to "feasted." The contest opened at a king's drinking feast where wine was called strongest (3:1-3, 17-23), and it closes with the exiles' own week-long feast of thanks. Wine is not the strongest thing, but the story does not forbid it: in its place it is joy (Psalm 104:15; Ecclesiastes 9:7).

a: Darius sent along a thousand horsemen
t: Compared with the Bible: an escort
p: Here Darius sends a thousand horsemen. Later Ezra is ashamed to ask a king for any.
b: This goes beyond Ezra, which tells of no escort for the first return. It also sits beside Ezra's own words: "I was ashamed to ask the king for a troop and horsemen" (Ezra 8:22; in this book, 1 Esdras 8:51), while Nehemiah does accept army officers and horsemen (Nehemiah 2:9). Josephus, retelling this chapter, says they went "under the conduct of those whom Darius sent along with them," with songs, pipes and cymbals, but he does not mention horsemen (Antiquities 11.67).

p: The Greek makes Joakim a son of Zerubbabel and lists him with the priests. The list may be damaged.
b: As it stands, the verse names two priests, Jeshua and "Joakim son of Zerubbabel," and then gives Joakim a royal line from David and Perez. But Zerubbabel was not a priest, and 1 Chronicles 3:19 names his sons as Meshullam and Hananiah. Nehemiah 12:10 says "Jeshua fathered Joiakim." So the words read like a damaged list, perhaps once "Joakim son of Jeshua" and "Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the house of David," with "who spoke wise words" (5:6) meant for Zerubbabel. The Greek runs 5:5 straight into 5:6 ("..., who spoke"); the Plain starts a new sentence, "He was the one," and like the Greek does not say whether "he" is Joakim or Zerubbabel. The KJV keeps the Greek, as the Plain does. Josephus names Zerubbabel and Jeshua as the leaders (Antiquities 11.73).

p: Jeshua's grandfather was the chief priest killed when Jerusalem fell.
b: 1 Chronicles 6:14-15 gives the line: Seraiah fathered Jehozadak (Jozadak), who went into exile. Seraiah was the chief priest whom the Babylonians took to Riblah and killed (2 Kings 25:18-21). Ezra calls Jeshua "son of Jozadak" (Ezra 3:2); 1 Esdras adds the grandfather, so the high priesthood is shown unbroken across the exile. Ezra himself is also called a son (descendant) of Seraiah (Ezra 7:1).

a: in the second year of his reign
p: Darius's second year, in Nisan. Haggai's first message is dated to the same year; Josephus puts the contest in the first.
b: Haggai's first message to Zerubbabel came "in the second year of King Darius" (Haggai 1:1), and the founding he speaks of was in its ninth month (Haggai 2:18). Nisan is the first month of the Jewish year, in spring. Josephus places the feast and contest "in the first year of the king's reign" (Antiquities 11.33). Note that 5:52 counts vows "since the new moon of the first month," the month of the contest.

a: He was the one who spoke wise words
t: Compared with the Bible: a return under Darius
p: Ezra puts Zerubbabel's return under Cyrus. 1 Esdras puts it under Darius, then follows Ezra's order anyway.
b: This conflicts with the order of Ezra. In Ezra the list of returnees (Ezra 2) follows Cyrus's decree (Ezra 1), and the altar and foundation are laid under Cyrus (Ezra 3:1-4:5). 1 Esdras has set the same list after the contest under Darius, yet keeps Ezra's words that the work stopped "the whole time King Cyrus was alive... until Darius became king" (5:70). Read as one story, 5:7-70 looks back at the first return. Torrey (1910) saw instead two documents joined, with the words of 5:6 as the patch between them, and Swete noted that the scene shifts "from Darius back again to Cyrus." See the note on 5:70.

a: where they had lived as strangers
p: The Greek says the exiles had been "sojourners," foreigners living in another land.
b: Ezra 2:1 has "out of captivity, from the exile" (Hebrew golah). The Greek here has tēs aichmalōsias tēs paroikias, "the captivity of the sojourning." Paroikia is the word for living as a resident foreigner, as Abraham did in Canaan and Israel in Egypt (Acts 13:17); 1 Peter 1:17 calls Christians' life on earth "the time of your sojourning." From here to 5:70 the Plain follows the site's Ezra 2:1-4:5 wherever the Greek says the same thing.

p: Ezra lists eleven leaders; 1 Esdras and Nehemiah list twelve. The names are Greek forms of the Hebrew ones.
b: Ezra 2:2 has eleven names, Nehemiah 7:7 twelve, adding Nahamani. 1 Esdras also has twelve, and Enenius stands where Nehemiah has Nahamani. The other names are Greek forms of those in Ezra 2:2: Zaraias for Seraiah, Resaias for Reelaiah, Beelsarus for Bilshan, Aspharasus for Mispar, Borolius for Bigvai, Roimus for Rehum, Baana for Baanah. Nehemiah and Mordecai here are not the governor Nehemiah or Esther's cousin; the names were common. See the note on Ezra 2:2.

a: The number of those from the nation
p: Names and numbers often differ from Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7. The Plain follows Vaticanus, with the Hebrew forms in the notes.
b: The list of 5:9-45 is the third copy of the list in Ezra 2:1-70 and Nehemiah 7:6-73, and the three disagree in many numbers. 1 Esdras also adds clans (5:15, 20) and lacks others (the other Elam and Harim, Ezra 2:31-32). Lists of names and numbers were easy to miscopy. The Plain follows Codex Vaticanus (Swete's text) in names and numbers even where a figure cannot be right, like 72,000 here for one clan, more than the 42,360 of the whole people (5:41); the other witnesses are in the variants. It leaves Vaticanus in one place only, 5:28, where the line cannot be read as a list at all, because its parts add up to more than its own total. Names are spelled from the Greek, with a rough breathing written as H (Hannis, Hobbia), except names English Bibles already spell one way (Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Mordecai, Asaph, Hezekiah). The totals in 5:41 agree with Ezra.

p: Iolamus is Elam, Zaton is Zattu, Chorbe is Zaccai, Bani is Bani.
b: The Greek forms in 5:9-23 match Ezra 2:3-35 in order: Phoros = Parosh, Ares = Arah, Phthalimoab = Pahath-moab, Roboab = Joab, Iolamus = Elam, Zaton = Zattu, Chorbe = Zaccai, Bebai = Bebai, Argai = Azgad, Adonikam, Bosai = Bigvai, Adilius = Adin, Azer of Hezekiah = Ater of Hezekiah, Bassai = Bezai, Ragethlomon = Bethlehem, Netebas = Netophah, Enatus = Anathoth, Baitasmon = Beth-azmaveth, Kartathiarius = Kiriath-jearim, Berog = Beeroth, Kirama Kabbes = Ramah and Geba, Makalon = Michmash, Betolio = Bethel (with the number of Nebo, 52), Niphis = Magbish's number (156), Kalamokalus and Onus = Lod, Hadid and Ono, Jerechus = Jericho, Sama = Senaah. Kilan and Azetas (5:15), Azarus (5:15), Hannis (5:16), Baiterus (5:17) and the Chadiasai and Hammidioi (5:20) have no clear match. Vaticanus has no line for Ezra's Shephatiah (Ezra 2:4); see the variant on 5:9.

p: Ezra has 666, Nehemiah 667, Codex Alexandrinus 647, and Vaticanus 37.
b: The four witnesses give four numbers for one clan: Ezra 2:13 has 666, Nehemiah 7:18 has 667, Codex Alexandrinus 647, and Codex Vaticanus (the Plain) 37. The famous number in Ezra has drawn readers to compare it with Revelation 13:18; see the note "666 again?" on Ezra 2:13. Here it shows only how easily copyists lost or changed the hundreds in a list of figures.

p: These two groups are found only in 1 Esdras. The list gives no clue to where they lived.
b: Ezra and Nehemiah have nothing between Beeroth and Ramah. The Greek names look like the names of people from places, "the Chadiasans and the Hammidians." Codex Alexandrinus, as far as Swete could read it, spells the first Kad'asai, and it has Ammidaioi for the second. The Plain transliterates.

p: The four priestly clans match Ezra 2:36-39, but with other numbers and a name Ezra lacks.
b: Jeddu son of Jeshua is Jedaiah "of the house of Jeshua" (Ezra 2:36); Ermerus is Immer, Phassorus Pashhur, Charme Harim. Sanabis has no match in the priest list (compare Senaah, 5:23 and Ezra 2:35). The numbers differ: 872 for 973, 252 for 1,052, 217 for 1,017; only Pashhur's 1,247 agrees. See the note "Many priests, few Levites" on Ezra 2:36.

p: The Greek hieropsaltai means "sacred singers"; Ezra has just "the singers."
b: Hieropsaltēs joins hieros, "sacred, of the temple," and psaltēs, a singer to the harp. 1 Esdras uses it for the Levite singers through the book (5:45 and later). Ezra 2:41 has plain meshorerim, "singers." The Plain says "temple singers."

p: The Greek word hierodouloi meant slaves owned by a temple. Ezra's Hebrew means "the given ones."
b: Ezra's netinim, "those given" to the temple, are rendered "temple servants" across the site (see the note on Ezra 2:43). 1 Esdras uses hierodouloi, "sacred slaves," the word Greeks used for people owned by a temple and bound to its service. The Plain keeps "temple servants" for the same group. The names are Greek forms of Ezra 2:43-57: Esau for Ziha (a Greek spelling, not the patriarch Esau), Tasipha for Hasupha, Keras for Keros, Sua for Siaha, Phalaeus for Padon, and so on.

a: Their leaders were Charaathalan and Allar
p: Ezra 2:59 lists five places in Babylonia. Here two of them have become the group's leaders.
b: Ezra 2:59 says these came "from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan and Immer," all villages in Babylonia. The Greek keeps the first two as places (Thermeleth, Thelersas) and turns Cherub and Addan into one name, Charaathalan, and Immer into Allar, "their leaders." Codex Alexandrinus splits it differently (Chara, Athalar and Alar). It is one of several places where the Greek writer read a Hebrew list of places as a list of people (compare 5:40, where a title becomes a name).

p: Only 1 Esdras gives the wife's name, Augia. In Ezra the man is Barzillai.
b: Ezra 2:61 says a priest "had married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and went by their name," so he was called Barzillai. Here he is Jaddus, his wife is named Augia, and her father is Phaezeldaeus, a garbled form of Barzillai (Codex Alexandrinus has Zorzelleus). Barzillai the Gileadite was David's loyal friend (2 Samuel 19:31-39). The point is the same in both books: a priest who took his wife's family name could not prove his own priestly line.

p: Ezra's "the governor" (Hebrew hattirshata) has become a man, Hattharias, with a Naimias beside him.
b: Ezra 2:63 and Nehemiah 7:65 have hattirshata, a Persian title, "His Excellency, the governor" (see the note on Ezra 2:63). The Greek writer took it as a name, Hattharias, and added Naimias (Codex Alexandrinus: Neemias, that is, Nehemiah). He may have been led by Nehemiah 8:9, where "Nehemiah, who was the governor" uses the same Hebrew title. Read as Alexandrinus spells it, the line puts Nehemiah in Zerubbabel's time, though Nehemiah's own book sets his work in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes (Nehemiah 2:1). The KJV has "Nehemias and Atharias."

t: The Urim and Thummim as "Showing and Truth"
p: The Greek Bible's names for the Urim and Thummim. Truth appears once more, now on the high priest's breastpiece.
b: The Hebrew has "the Urim and the Thummim," the lots the high priest carried in his breastpiece to learn God's will (Exodus 28:30). The Greek of Exodus renders them tēn dēlōsin kai tēn alētheian, "the Showing and the Truth" (Exodus 28:26 in Swete's Greek), and 1 Esdras uses the same words. So the word that won the contest (4:41) returns here as the sign of a priest who can give God's true answer. The votive Mass for the election of a pope, as printed in a set of Latin-English parish propers, gives this verse as its offertory, citing "3 Esdræ 5:40": Non participentur sancta, donec exsurgat pontifex in ostensionem et veritatem, with pontifex, "high priest" (see the variant).
orig: τὴν δήλωσιν καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν (tēn dēlōsin kai tēn alētheian)

a: Israel from twelve years old and up
p: The total, 42,360, agrees with Ezra and Nehemiah. 1 Esdras adds that it counts those twelve and older.
b: The grand total matches Ezra 2:64 and Nehemiah 7:66, though the clan numbers above do not add up to it, as in Ezra (see the note "A total that is too big" on Ezra 2:64). Only 1 Esdras says the count was from age twelve up. The 7,337 slaves match Ezra 2:65; the 245 singers match Nehemiah 7:67 (Ezra 2:65 has 200). Josephus repeats the 7,337 servants and 245 singers (Antiquities 11.72).

p: Ezra has 736 horses; 1 Esdras has 7,036, and pack animals for Ezra's donkeys.
b: Camels (435) and mules (245) agree with Ezra 2:66-67. The horses here are 7,036 against Ezra's 736, perhaps a copying slip in the thousands, and "pack animals," 5,525, stand where Ezra has 6,720 donkeys. Josephus gives 435 camels and 5,525 beasts of burden, following this book (Antiquities 11.72).

p: Ezra counts the gold in drachmas, 61,000. 1 Esdras counts it in minas, 1,000.
b: Ezra 2:69 has 61,000 drachmas (or darics) of gold, 5,000 minas of silver and 100 priests' robes; Nehemiah 7:70-72 splits the gifts among the governor, the family heads and the people. 1 Esdras agrees on the silver and the robes, but counts the gold in minas, 1,000 of them. The two books use different measures for the gold, so their figures cannot simply be set side by side. In 1 Esdras the gifts are also vowed, not handed over (5:43).

a: the open square of the first gate, the one facing east
t: The square by the east gate
p: Ezra says only "at Jerusalem." 1 Esdras names a square by the east gate, where in this book Ezra will later read the law.
b: Ezra 3:1 says the people "gathered at Jerusalem." 1 Esdras places them in the open square of the first gate facing east. At the end of the book the people gather again "in the open square before the east gate of the temple" to hear Ezra read the law (9:38), which Nehemiah places "in the open square facing the Water Gate" (Nehemiah 8:1). In this book the square links its two great gatherings, the altar and the law, by one place.

a: People from the other nations of the land gathered to them
p: Ezra says the builders feared the peoples. The Greek seems to say some foreigners joined them, though they were hostile.
b: Ezra 3:3: "They set the altar firmly on its old base, because dread of the peoples of the lands was on them." The Greek here is hard. Episynēchthēsan autois most naturally means "gathered to them" (joined them), as the KJV takes it; it could also mean "gathered against them." The next clauses give the reason for setting up the altar: "for they were hostile to them," and all the nations were stronger. The Greek does not name who "they" are, and the Plain keeps that open; the next clause, about the nations, suggests the nations. The first clause can be read of converts or neighbors coming to the altar (compare Ezra 6:21), or of hostile crowds. Josephus says the neighboring nations "bare an ill-will to them" (Antiquities 11.76).

p: Where Ezra's Plain has "the LORD" and the Greek has Kyrios, this part keeps "the LORD."
b: Greek has no divine name; Kyrios, "Lord," stands for the Hebrew YHWH. Because 1 Esdras 5:46-70 retells Ezra 3:1-4:5, the Plain keeps "the LORD" where the site's Ezra has it and the Greek has Kyrios (see the note at 1:1). Where the Greek has Kyrios but Ezra has "God" or nothing, the Plain says "the Lord" (5:56, 66-67). In chapters 3-4, outside any parallel, God is "the King of heaven," "the God of truth" and "Master."

p: Ezra lists the regular offering, new moons and feasts. 1 Esdras adds the Sabbaths.
b: Ezra 3:5 lists the regular burnt offering, the new moons, "all the LORD's holy set feasts," and freewill offerings. 1 Esdras adds the Sabbath sacrifices, as the law requires (Numbers 28:9-10), and turns the freewill offerings into the vows of 5:52. The Greek's "regular offerings" (endelechismos, "continual") is the Greek Bible's term for the daily offering (Exodus 29:42).

a: On the new moon of the second month
p: 1 Esdras dates it exactly; Ezra gives only the month; Haggai and Zechariah put it under Darius.
b: Ezra 3:8-10 says the work began in the second month of the second year and the builders founded the temple, without a day; Ezra 5:16 credits Sheshbazzar with laying the foundations; Haggai 2:18 names "the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month" of Darius's second year; Zechariah 4:9 says Zerubbabel's hands founded the house. 1 Esdras adds a day, the new moon (first day) of the second month, and since it has placed the return under Darius (5:6), its "second year" falls in Darius's reign, closer to Haggai. See the note "When was the foundation laid?" on Ezra 3:8.

p: Damadiel is Kadmiel; "Emadabun" is Henadad; "Judah son of Iliadun" is Ezra's "sons of Judah."
b: Ezra 3:9 names Jeshua with his sons and brothers, Kadmiel and his sons, "the sons of Judah," and the sons of Henadad. The Greek has the same names in other forms and other links: Damadiel (Codex Alexandrinus: Kadoel) for Kadmiel, "the sons of Jeshua Emadabun" for the sons of Henadad, and "Judah son of Iliadun." The Jeshua here is the Levite of 5:26 and Ezra 2:40, not the high priest.

a: For his kindness and glory last forever, for all Israel
p: Ezra's "for he is good, for his loyal love... is forever" becomes "kindness and glory."
b: The song of Ezra 3:11 is the refrain of Psalm 136: "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, / for his loyal love is forever" (Psalm 136:1), also sung when the ark came to Jerusalem and at Solomon's temple (1 Chronicles 16:34; 2 Chronicles 7:3) and promised by Jeremiah for the return (Jeremiah 33:11). The Greek here has chrēstotēs, "kindness, goodness," and adds doxa, "glory," in place of Hebrew hesed, "loyal love."

a: so that the people could not hear the trumpets over the people's weeping
p: In Ezra no one can tell joy from weeping. In 1 Esdras, and in Josephus, the weeping drowns the trumpets.
b: Ezra 3:13 says "No one could tell the glad shouting apart from the weeping." The Greek says the weeping kept the people from hearing the trumpets, though the trumpets were heard far off. Josephus tells it the same way: the old men's and priests' weeping drowned the sound of the trumpets and the rejoicing (Antiquities 11.83). The old men had seen Solomon's temple (Haggai 2:3). Either way the day held both grief and joy.

a: the enemies of the tribe of Judah and Benjamin
p: Josephus calls them Cuthites, that is, Samaritans.
b: The enemies say they were brought to the land by an Assyrian king (5:66), so they are the peoples settled in the old northern kingdom after its fall (2 Kings 17:24-41). Josephus calls them the Samaritans, also called Cuthites from Cuthah (Antiquities 11.84-85). See the note "Who were the 'enemies'?" on Ezra 4:1.

p: Ezra names Esarhaddon. The Greek forms here are garbled; Josephus names Shalmaneser.
b: Ezra 4:2 has Esarhaddon, the Assyrian king who, the neighbors say, brought them there. Codex Vaticanus has Asbakaphath, Codex Alexandrinus Asbasareth, both garbled forms; the KJV's Azbazareth comes from the second. Josephus names "Shalmanezer, the king of Assyria" (Antiquities 11.85), the king of 2 Kings 17:3. The neighbors also say they "heed" (akouomen, "hear, obey") the Lord, where Ezra has "we seek your God."

p: The Greek makes the refusal sharper: "we alone," where Ezra's Hebrew says "we together."
b: Ezra 4:3 has anachnu yachad, "we ourselves, together." The Greek has hēmeis monoi, "we alone." The meaning is close, since both shut the neighbors out, but the Greek puts the stress on exclusion. Josephus adds that the neighbors might still come to worship at the temple, but not help build it (Antiquities 11.86-87).

a: lay heavy on the people in Judea
p: The Greek verb is odd: "lying down upon." It pictures an enemy camped on the people.
b: Epikoimaomai is "to lie down on, to sleep upon." Together with poliorkountes, "besieging," it pictures the neighbors as an army camped around Judea, where Ezra 4:4 speaks of weakening the people's hands and frightening them. The KJV has "lying heavy upon."

p: The book has just put Zerubbabel's return in Darius's reign. Now it says the work stopped until Darius.
b: Chapters 3-4 put Zerubbabel at Darius's court, and 5:6 dates his return to Darius's second year. Yet the building was stopped "the whole time King Cyrus was alive... until Darius became king" (5:70, following Ezra 4:5), and chapter 6 begins in Darius's second year as if the story had not yet reached him. 1 Esdras also adds "for two years." Torrey (1910) explained the knot as a seam: the contest (3:1-5:6) was set into an older history, with 5:6 as the patch. Read as one story, the writer looks back from Darius to tell how the first return fared under Cyrus; Swete noted that the scene moves "from Darius back again to Cyrus." Josephus solves it by placing the hindrance under Cyrus and Cambyses (Antiquities 11.88).
